title: The Living Room and the Ordinary Disciple: Making Disciples Without a Program
subtitle: The regular, untrained believer is not a spectator in the work of making disciples. He is the worker Jesus chose. What Scripture, church history, and honest research say about why disciple-making happens in living rooms and over coffee rather than in classrooms and programs, and how an ordinary person with no degree and no special gift can begin this week with a life, a couch, and a few people over time.

parts.title: The Work You Assumed Was Not Yours
parts.body:
You assume someone else does this. When you hear the words make disciples, your mind goes immediately to the people who are qualified, the pastor, the staff, the small group leader who went through the training, the woman who knows her Bible cold and never seems afraid. You file yourself among the helped rather than the helpers, the discipled rather than the disciplers, and you have done it so long it no longer feels like a decision. It feels like a fact about you. Disciple-making is for the professionals, and you are not one.

So you have lived your whole Christian life on the receiving end. You attend, you listen, you absorb. You are a consumer of a thing other people produce, and the quiet message of nearly every church you have belonged to has confirmed it, that the real ministry happens up front, done by trained people, and your job is to show up, support it, and invite your friends to come watch the experts. You believe in the priesthood of all believers as a doctrine. You have never once lived as if you were a priest.

And underneath the assumption is fear, the specific fear of the unequipped. What if they ask a question I cannot answer. What if I say it wrong. What if I am exposed as someone who does not know enough, has not read enough, has too many doubts and too thin a faith to be handing it to anyone else. You look at your own struggling, ordinary, half-finished walk with God and you conclude that a person like you has no business trying to form anyone. You would only do damage. Better to leave it to the people who have it together.

Let me name the lie under all of it, because it has crippled the church for a century. The lie is that disciple-making is a specialized skill possessed by trained professionals and performed inside institutions. It is not. It never was. It is the most ordinary thing in the world, a believer sharing the life of Christ with a few people over time, in the place where life actually happens, which is not a classroom. It is a living room. You do not need a degree, a gift you were not given, or anyone's permission. You need a life, a couch, a pot of coffee, and a few people you are willing to walk with. You were qualified the day you were saved, and the church told you a story that benched you for years.

parts.title: Why the Professionals Cannot Reach the People You Can
parts.body:
The stakes begin with a math problem the church has refused to solve. There are too few professionals and far too many people. If disciple-making belongs only to pastors and trained staff, then the work is capped at the number of paid experts a congregation can afford, which is a tiny fraction of the people who need a disciple-maker, and so most people get none. We have built a system that guarantees scarcity, then we call the scarcity normal. The early church did the opposite. It assumed every believer was a worker, and so it had as many disciple-makers as it had disciples, and that is the only arithmetic that has ever filled a city.

The stakes deepen when you see that the professional cannot reach the people you can. Your pastor does not know your coworker, has never met your neighbor, will never sit in your brother-in-law's kitchen at eleven at night when the marriage is falling apart. You will. The lost and the seeking are not waiting in church lobbies for trained staff to find them. They are standing in your driveway, sitting at the desk beside yours, raising kids on your street, and they are reachable only by the Christian who already shares their ordinary life. The professional is a stranger to them. You are not. The whole strategy of reaching people through experts in buildings fails precisely where it matters most, at the edges, where the church does not yet touch and only an ordinary believer ever will.

The stakes are sharpest in a post-Christian America, where the old assumptions have quietly collapsed. For generations we could trust that the institution carried the weight, that people would come to the building, respect the office, and receive the faith through professional channels. That world is gone. Your neighbor will not come to your church, has no warm feeling toward the office of pastor, and is deeply suspicious of institutions of every kind. But that same neighbor will trust a friend. In a culture that has lost faith in experts and platforms, the most credible witness left is an ordinary person living an ordinary life of faith out in the open, and that witness is not a fallback for when the professionals fail. It is the front line, and you are standing on it whether you wanted to be or not.

And the stakes are generational, because a disciple formed by a professional learns that disciple-making requires being a professional. He concludes, watching, that this work takes a degree he does not have and a platform he will never build, and so the chain ends with him. But a disciple formed by an ordinary believer in a living room learns that disciple-making requires only what he already possesses, a home, a faith, and a few people, and so he goes and does the same, and his disciple does the same, and the thing multiplies. The professional model adds. The ordinary model multiplies. That is the difference between a church that maintains a building and a movement that cannot be stopped, and it turns entirely on whether the regular believer believes the work is his.

parts.title: How God Filled the Earth With Ordinary People
parts.body:
Look at who Jesus chose, because it is the first answer to your fear. He did not recruit the scholars of Jerusalem or the trained men of the temple. He called fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot, men with no theological credentials and no standing, and he made them the foundation of everything that followed. When the rulers later examined Peter and John, Luke records exactly what they saw, that these men were uneducated and ordinary, and that they had been with Jesus. There it is in one sentence. The qualification was never the education. It was the time spent with him. Jesus deliberately built his whole movement on regular people so that no one could ever say the work belonged to the experts, because there were no experts. There were only ordinary men who had been with Jesus, and that is precisely what you are.

Then watch how the gospel actually spread, because it was not the apostles who carried it furthest. In Acts 8, a wave of persecution scatters the church out of Jerusalem, and Luke tells us that those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Then he adds, almost in passing, except the apostles. The professionals stayed in the city. It was the nameless, ordinary, scattered believers, refugees with no title and no commission beyond their baptism, who carried the gospel across the region as they fled, gossiping the good news in whatever house took them in. The greatest expansion in the book of Acts was accomplished by people whose names we will never know, doing the most untrained thing imaginable, telling their neighbors about Jesus on the run.

Follow them to Antioch, and the pattern becomes a principle. In Acts 11, some of those scattered believers, ordinary men from Cyprus and Cyrene, arrive in a great pagan city and simply begin speaking to Greeks about the Lord Jesus, and Luke says the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed. This is the church at Antioch, the congregation that would soon send out Paul himself, the launching point of the whole Gentile mission, and it was founded not by an apostle, not by a strategy, not by a program, but by anonymous laypeople who saw a city full of people who did not know Jesus and started talking. The headquarters of the world mission began as a few ordinary believers sharing their faith in a place where no professional had thought to go.

And Peter, the uneducated fisherman, wrote the verses that name what God had done to people like you. You are a chosen race, he says, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light. A royal priesthood. Not a congregation served by priests, but a people every one of whom is a priest, with direct access to God and a direct commission to proclaim him. In the old covenant the priesthood was a class, a few qualified men who alone could approach God and mediate him to others. In the new covenant Peter declares the class dissolved and the office given to everyone, the maid and the farmer and the tradesman, all of them priests now, all of them carriers of the holy thing. You were not left out of the priesthood. You were made a member of it the day you believed.

And this is the deepest grain of how God has always worked, that he loves to fill the earth with his glory through the unqualified, so the glory is unmistakably his. God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, Paul wrote, and what is weak to shame the strong, and what is low and despised, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no human being might boast in his presence. The pattern runs from Gideon's three hundred to David's sling to a virgin's womb to twelve fishermen, and it runs straight to you, sitting in your living room, certain you are not enough. The certainty is the qualification. God does his largest work through people exactly that ordinary, on purpose, so that when the harvest comes in no one can mistake whose strength brought it. You are not the exception to how God works. You are the rule.

parts.title: Every Renewal Put the Work Back in Ordinary Hands
parts.body:
Read the honest historians of the early church and you find them puzzling over the same fact, that a movement with no buildings, no clergy class for generations, no public standing, and no institutional machinery managed to grow from a handful of Galileans into a faith that filled the Roman Empire in under three centuries. The answer they keep arriving at is unspectacular and decisive. It spread through ordinary believers, in their homes, along the ordinary channels of family, friendship, and trade. The faith moved the way news moves through a neighborhood, from person to person, household to household, conversation to conversation, carried by people whose only credential was that they had been changed and could not stop talking about it. There was no other engine. There did not need to be one.

Then came the centuries when the work was slowly taken out of ordinary hands. As the church grew, formal, and powerful, ministry hardened into a profession, a clergy set apart and elevated, and the laity were gradually reduced to spectators, recipients of a sacred work performed by experts on their behalf. By the late Middle Ages the ordinary believer had no Bible in his own tongue, no voice in the church's life, and no conception that the work of God might be his to do. The priesthood had become a class again, exactly the arrangement Peter had declared abolished, and a thousand years of passivity was the result.

Then, in 1520, a monk named Martin Luther wrote a treatise to the German nobility and put a hammer to the whole edifice. There is no true, basic difference between laymen and priests, he wrote, between religious and secular, except for the sake of office and work, for all Christians whatsoever really and truly belong to the spiritual estate. He recovered the doctrine the church had buried, the priesthood of all believers, and its consequences were seismic. If every Christian is a priest, then the farmer at his plow and the wife at her washing are doing holy work, and the proclaiming of the gospel and the discipling of souls is not the property of an ordained class but the common calling of the baptized. Luther put the Bible in the people's language and the ministry back in the people's hands, and he did it on the conviction that the ordinary believer is not a lesser Christian served by the real ones, but a priest of God himself.

Two centuries later, John Wesley proved the doctrine could fill a nation. As the revival broke out across England in the 1740s, Wesley faced a problem the professionals could not solve. There were far more awakened souls than there were trained clergy to shepherd them, and the established church was largely closed to him. So he did the radical thing. He gathered the new believers into small groups called classes, a dozen or so meeting weekly in a home, and over each one he placed an ordinary, untrained believer as the class leader, a tradesman or a servant or a laboring woman whose only job was to ask each member how their soul was faring, to pray with them, and to watch over them in love. Wesley was scandalized at first by the idea of unordained people leading. He came to see it as the genius of the whole movement. These lay class leaders, thousands of them, ordinary Christians discipling their neighbors in their front rooms, were the structure that turned a revival into a reformation of the English people. The fire spread because Wesley refused to keep the work in professional hands.

And the lesson has been relearned in every awakening since, because it is the lesson the church forgets first whenever it grows comfortable. Wherever the gospel has multiplied rather than merely maintained itself, you find the same pattern, the work returned to the ordinary believer, the living room reopened as the place of formation, the priesthood of all believers taken not as a slogan but as a job description. And wherever the church has stalled and shrunk, you find the opposite, ministry professionalized, the laity benched, the work locked inside institutions that fewer and fewer people will enter. We are not waiting for a new strategy. We are waiting to remember an old one, that God works through ordinary people, and the renewal always comes when somebody believes it again.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: How movements actually grow, how ordinary people actually learn complex things, and how influence actually travels through a society are questions researchers have studied with care, and a believer can receive what they have found gratefully and critically at once, because all truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of how ordinary people spread an idea carries a hidden picture of what a person is and what is finally moving them, and the picture is where the wisdom is won or lost.

secular.source: The Tipping Point and the dynamics of social epidemics
secular.author: Malcolm Gladwell
secular.whatItGetsRight: Gladwell showed that ideas and behaviors spread not chiefly through institutions and advertising but through ordinary people connected to one another, that a small number of well-networked, ordinary individuals can carry a message through a whole population, and that word of mouth from a trusted peer remains the most powerful force for change there is. This is a precise secular description of how the early church multiplied, person to person along ordinary relationships, and it confirms that the regular believer in his living room is positioned at the most powerful point in any network of influence.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Gladwell accurately maps the channel and is silent on the One who moves through it. His analysis can show that ordinary people spread ideas through relationships and treats the spreading as a social mechanism, when Scripture insists that the increase belongs to God, who alone gives the growth while Paul plants and Apollos waters. The hand of the Lord was with the ordinary believers at Antioch, Luke says, and that hand is the thing no network theory can see. The research rightly recovers the relational, person-to-person shape of how the gospel travels. It cannot account for the new birth that no social epidemic can manufacture and only the Spirit can give.

secular.source: Situated learning and legitimate peripheral participation
secular.author: Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger
secular.whatItGetsRight: Lave and Wenger demonstrated that people learn complex practices not by formal instruction but by participating in a community of practice, beginning at the edges and moving inward as they share the life of those already skilled, so that the untrained newcomer becomes competent simply by belonging and doing alongside others over time. This dismantles the assumption that real learning requires a classroom and an expert, and it describes exactly how Jesus formed the twelve and how an ordinary believer disciples another, by sharing a life rather than delivering a lecture.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research illuminates the shape of formation and cannot supply its center. It explains how a newcomer becomes like the community he joins, and Scripture says the one we are being conformed to is Christ and the power is the Spirit, not merely the belonging. A person can participate at the edges of a Christian community for years and learn only its customs if the Spirit does not give the life. The science rightly recovers the truth that disciples are formed by shared practice rather than transferred information. The gospel names whose life is being reproduced in us and who is doing the reproducing.

secular.source: Diffusion of Innovations and how new practices spread
secular.author: Everett Rogers
secular.whatItGetsRight: Rogers, studying how new ideas and practices move through a population, found that people adopt them overwhelmingly on the testimony of trusted peers who are like themselves rather than on the recommendation of distant experts, and that the most persuasive evidence is watching someone in your own circle live the new thing first. This explains why an ordinary believer's witness outperforms a professional's, and why a faith caught from a friend at the kitchen table spreads where an argument from an authority figure does not.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Rogers rightly names the power of the trusted peer and reaches the edge of conversion without crossing it. His research can show that people adopt a practice when someone like them models it and cannot account for a change that goes deeper than any practice, the turning of a heart from death to life. Scripture welcomes the witness of the ordinary peer, Andrew finding his brother, the Samaritan woman running to her town, and it insists the drawing is the Father's, that no one comes unless the Father draws him. The model rightly recovers the persuasive weight of an ordinary life lived openly. It cannot reach the regeneration that only God performs.

secular.source: The research on weak ties and the strength of ordinary acquaintance
secular.author: Mark Granovetter
secular.whatItGetsRight: Granovetter showed that new information and opportunity travel into our lives most often not through our closest relationships but through our weaker ties, the acquaintances, neighbors, and coworkers who connect us to circles our intimate friends do not reach. This means the ordinary believer's wide field of casual relationships, the people he merely waves to, is the very network through which the gospel is most likely to reach genuinely new ground, and it dignifies the unremarkable acquaintances of an ordinary life as a frontier of mission.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The research honors the reach of ordinary acquaintance and must be held with care, lest mission become a matter of efficient networking. Scripture sends the believer not to harvest his contacts but to love his neighbor, and the loving is the point whether or not the tie ever bears fruit. Jesus crossed a social tie to a despised Samaritan woman and gave her his full attention, not as a node in a network but as a soul before him. The science rightly recovers the missional value of the wide, ordinary web of relationships. The gospel keeps the person at the end of the tie from being reduced to a means.

secular.source: The sociology of religious movement growth
secular.author: Rodney Stark
secular.whatItGetsRight: Stark, analyzing how the early church and other movements actually grew, established with hard data that religious movements spread through the ordinary social bonds of ordinary members, that rank-and-file believers sharing their faith within their existing relationships, not professional missionaries or mass campaigns, account for nearly all sustainable growth. His work is a direct rebuke to the professional model, demonstrating that the engine of expansion has always been the regular believer embedded in a network of family, friends, and neighbors.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Stark rightly identifies the ordinary believer as the engine and reaches the limit of what sociology can see. He can measure that movements grow through the relationships of regular members and cannot weigh the prayer, the Spirit, and the cost that Scripture places at the center of the church's growth. The believers scattered in Acts 8 were not running a growth strategy. They were fleeing persecution and could not stop preaching Christ. The research rightly dignifies the ordinary member as the true agent of the church's spread. The gospel reveals that the spread is finally the Lord adding to his church those who are being saved.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who equally affirm that every believer is a priest and a disciple-maker still differ on how that calling relates to the trained ministry of the church, and each emphasis guards against a real failure it has watched happen. The dividing question is whether the ordinary believer should simply be released to make disciples in his own way or whether his work should be deliberately equipped and ordered by the church's trained ministry. Hear each view at its strongest, because the wisest practitioners hold both and the difference is mostly one of where the weight should fall.

views.view: Release the ordinary believer: trust the priesthood of all
views.body: This view holds that the church's first task is simply to release ordinary believers into the work and get out of their way, because the priesthood of all believers means the regular Christian is already qualified and the chief obstacle is not his lack of training but the institution's reluctance to trust him. It takes seriously that the early church multiplied through scattered laypeople with no oversight, that Wesley's revival turned on handing the work to untrained class leaders, and that every wave of professionalizing has benched the people and choked the growth. So this view pushes hard against gatekeeping, against the endless trainings and certifications that imply the ordinary believer is not ready, and it tells the fearful Christian the plain truth, that he has a life and a living room and the Spirit of God, and that is enough to begin today. Advocates argue that the church has discipled its people into passivity by always implying the real work requires more preparation than they have, and that the cure is to believe Peter, that they are a royal priesthood now, and to send them. The failure they are guarding against is real, a clericalism that hoards ministry, keeps the laity dependent, and produces consumers who wait forever to be qualified for a work they were qualified for at their baptism. They are quick to add that releasing the ordinary believer is not abandoning him, that he still needs the Word, the church, and the company of the wise, and that freedom without any formation can drift into error and burnout if the released believer is not also being fed.

views.view: Equip the ordinary believer: order the work through the church
views.body: This view holds that the ordinary believer should indeed make disciples, and that the church's job is to equip and order that work so it is healthy, faithful, and sustained, because zeal without knowledge does damage and a released believer who is never equipped can teach error, burn out, or lead people astray with the best intentions. It takes seriously that Scripture gives the church pastors and teachers precisely to equip the saints for the work of ministry, that the work belongs to the saints and the equipping belongs to the trained, so the two are not rivals but partners. So this view invests in forming ordinary believers well, in grounding them in Scripture, in giving them a simple reproducible pattern, in connecting their living rooms to the wider body so they are supported rather than isolated. Advocates argue that the church has too often swung from clericalism to a careless populism that sends untrained people out with nothing and calls the resulting confusion freedom, and that real multiplication requires not just permission but preparation. The failure they are guarding against is real, a do-it-yourself discipleship that, cut off from the church's teaching and oversight, drifts into shallowness, error, or the cult of a charismatic amateur. They are quick to add that equipping must never become a permanent gate that keeps the ordinary believer from ever beginning, that the goal of the equipping is precisely to send him, and an equipping that only ever prepares and never releases has missed the point as badly as the clericalism it fears.

parts.title: What This Work Forms in the One Who Begins It
parts.body:
When an ordinary believer finally steps across the line and begins to disciple another person, the first thing that happens is not what he expected. He set out to form someone else, and he discovers that the work is forming him, more deeply and more quickly than years of sitting and receiving ever did. The living room makes a disciple of the host, and this is the secret no one tells the fearful person who will not begin.

It forms courage, the particular courage of the unqualified who acts anyway. As long as you wait to feel ready, you stay a spectator, and the waiting feels like humility but is actually a kind of unbelief, a refusal to trust that God works through ordinary people. The moment you invite someone over and open the Bible despite your fear, you put your weight on the promise that the Spirit equips the willing, and the promise holds, and your faith grows muscle it could never grow on the sidelines. You learn in your body what you could not learn in your head, that he uses people exactly as unprepared as you, and the learning makes you brave.

It forms a faith that finally has to know what it believes. There is no teacher like the obligation to teach, no study like the question you cannot answer, no clarifier of your own convictions like a seeking friend across the coffee table asking why. The believer who only ever receives can stay vague forever, holding a faith he has never had to articulate. The believer who disciples another is driven back into Scripture with a new hunger, forced to find out what he actually believes and why, and his own faith deepens and settles in the very act of handing it to someone else. You will learn more of the gospel in a year of helping one person follow Jesus than in a decade of being a good audience.

It forms love for particular people rather than for the abstraction of mission. It is easy to believe in reaching the lost and hard to love the specific man in your living room who argues, doubts, relapses, and tells you the same story for the third time. The work puts a real person in front of you, with his real mess and his slow progress and his three steps back, and it sands away the romance until what is left is the patient, particular, inconvenient love that actually changes people. You find out you are far more selfish with your evenings and your home than you believed, and that finding is not the work failing. It is the work forming you.

And it forms a man in the image of his Master, until he understands the gospel from the inside. Jesus took ordinary, unqualified people and shared his life with them until they became like him, and every time you do the same, every time you take a fearful new believer or a searching neighbor and give him your time and your home and your honest, struggling faith, you are doing in miniature exactly what Jesus did for you, who did not wait until you were qualified but came and walked with you as you were. You cannot keep doing that without being changed by it, without the patience you are extending teaching you at last how patient was the One who extended it to you. That is the thing hidden at the center of the work. While you are giving your ordinary life away to make a disciple, the God who chose fishermen is quietly making one of you.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: This is the part the whole resource exists for, because the priesthood of all believers is not a doctrine to admire but a calling to live, and an ordinary person can live it starting this week. You do not need a curriculum, a credential, a gift you were not given, or anyone's permission. You need a life, a living room, a pot of coffee, and a willingness to share your actual faith with a few people over time. What follows is a concrete path from your first invitation to a reproducing rhythm that sends ordinary people out to disciple ordinary people. Begin small, begin afraid if you must, but begin.

steps: Settle the lie before you do anything else. Write down the real reason you have never tried to disciple anyone, not gifted enough, not trained enough, too many doubts, and then write beside it what Scripture says, that you are a royal priesthood and that Jesus built his church on uneducated, ordinary men who had simply been with him. Preach the truth to your fear until it loosens its grip, because the first obstacle is always inside you.

Pray over your actual circle and your actual living room. Ask God for one or two names, a new believer who needs a steadier friend, a neighbor who is asking real questions, a coworker who is lonely, a younger Christian who is stuck. You are not looking for a project. You are looking for the person God has already placed within your ordinary reach.

Make one ordinary invitation this week, with no program announced and nothing intimidating attached. Say plainly, come over for coffee, I would love to catch up. The point is to open your home and your life, not to launch a class, and the most spiritual thing you can do at the start is simply to get a real person onto your couch.

When they come, do not perform and do not preach. Ask about their life, listen far more than you talk, and let them see that your home is warm and your interest is real. Let the first visit do one job only, make them want to come back, because everything that follows grows out of an ordinary relationship that they actually enjoy.

Turn the visit into a rhythm by setting a regular time and protecting it like an appointment you cannot miss. The same person, the same living room, the same hour each week or each fortnight. Formation is the fruit of repetition, and the single most important decision you will make is to give this relationship a fixed and defended place in your week.

Begin to share your own faith honestly, as a natural part of your real life rather than a lesson you deliver. Talk about your week with God the way you talk about your week at work, mention what you are praying about, name a place you are struggling to trust him. Let them watch an ordinary, unfinished Christian be honest about following Jesus, because that sight does more than any polished answer.

Practice answering nothing and pointing to everything. When a question comes that you cannot answer, do not panic and do not fake it. Say the freeing, ordinary truth, I do not know, let us look at what the Bible says and find out together. You are not the expert and you do not need to be. You are a fellow traveler who knows the One worth following, and that posture disciples better than any expertise.

Invite them into your real life beyond the scheduled meeting. Have them over for a meal with your family, ask them to run an errand with you, let them see how you handle a frustration or a disappointment. Disciple-making is not an hour of content but the sharing of a life, and the ordinary, unscripted moments are where they learn the most about following Jesus.

Bring the Bible into the living room in the simplest way there is. After coffee, read a short passage together, a few verses from a Gospel, and ask three questions anyone can ask, what does this show us about God, what does it show us about ourselves, and what might it mean for this week. You do not teach. You open the book and let Jesus do the teaching while you learn alongside.

Add prayer to the rhythm, starting small enough that it does not intimidate either of you. Ask, how can I pray for you this week, write the answer down, and follow up next time to see what God did. Praying for someone by name and watching the answers come disciples them in the reality of God faster than any argument, and it is something even the most ordinary believer can do well.

Walk with them through the actual following, not just the learning. When they are ready, talk plainly about repentance, faith, baptism, obedience, the real shape of a life given to Jesus, and help them take the next step they are facing. Bring your own ordinary obedience into the open as the model, since you are not handing them a theory but inviting them into a life you are living a few steps ahead of them.

Watch for the day they could do this for someone else, and start naming it out loud. Tell them, what we are doing is the most ordinary thing in the world, and one day you will do it for someone too. Plant the expectation early that they are not only being fed but being equipped to feed, because a disciple who knows he is being prepared to disciple becomes a maker rather than a consumer.

Send your person out to start their own living room, with their own people, and resist the urge to keep them at yours forever. When they are ready, help them choose a name to invite, walk them through their first few meetings, and then step back. The goal is not the biggest possible group around you but the most ordinary believers discipling others across a city, and that only happens when you let people go.

Hand them a pattern simple enough to carry without you, the very pattern you used, a relationship, an open home, honest faith, a short passage with the three questions, and prayer. The reason the early church filled the empire is that its method required nothing an ordinary believer did not already have, and a way of making disciples that you can hand to anyone is a way that will outlive and outgrow you.

Stay connected to your church and the wise believers in it, so that your living-room work is fed and ordered rather than isolated. Bring your questions to your pastor, keep yourself under good teaching, and let the wider body support what you are doing in your home. Freedom to begin and equipping to continue are not enemies, and the ordinary disciple-maker who stays connected to the church lasts and stays faithful.

Keep your living room open for the long haul, through the seasons when someone is growing fast and the seasons when no one seems to respond, trusting God with a harvest you cannot force. Some you welcome will follow Jesus and some will drift, some you disciple will flourish and some will wander, and your task is not to control the outcome but to keep opening the door, pouring the coffee, and sharing the life, the way ordinary believers have done since the church was scattered out of Jerusalem, until the day you stand in a crowd no one could number and find faces in it that are there because a regular person with a living room finally believed the work was his.
